method: Independent source-visual solve; inferred option IDs and reasoning recorded before author answers, explanations or correct flags were opened. Option IDs retained from blinded packet; source pages 15–46 personally viewed.

answers.reasoning: The slide definition requires integration of mechanical, electrical and software components and reprogrammability; neither autonomy alone nor software alone is sufficient.
Human intervention is explicitly allowed by the definition; remote operation does not by itself disqualify a robot.
Robotics explicitly studies design, programming and control rather than a restricted application list.
The slide traces robot to Slavic words for work, compulsory work or drudgery.
The slide names Karel Čapek, R.U.R. and 1920; this is a source-reporting question.
The displayed year is 1962. This verifies the slide claim, not external historical accuracy.
The three linked source facts are Unimation, founders Engelberger and Devol, and the General Motors plant.
The caption labels Joseph F. Engelberger Father of Robotics.
The long-arm axial extension arrow is labeled Radial motion; the wrist and rotary arrows describe different rotations.
The slide pairs mobility with transport and manipulation with action on the environment.
The slide contrasts wheels on flat surfaces with legs for uneven terrain; this does not claim all wheels can never traverse uneven terrain.
The photo captions assign ROBOTINO to wheels and BIGDOG to legs.
All first three statements appear in the slide. Industrial teleoperation is explicitly permitted, so universal autonomy is false.
The classification list includes fixed/mobile, serial/parallel and rigid/flexible, but not customer payment method. The latter is an implausible giveaway distractor design.
Older industrial robots are described as fixed-base connected links with actuated joints.
The serial diagram is one sequential chain from base to end-effector, unlike the multiple legs of the parallel drawing.
Multiple extensible legs join the fixed lower base to the top platform in the parallel drawing.
A generic unconstrained rigid pose has three position and three orientation coordinates, yielding six under the stated task convention.
The source examples explicitly give four-DOF SCARA electronic assembly and five-DOF painting/welding tasks, not a universal constraint on every application.
Extra DOF allow redundant movement to avoid obstacles. They do not eliminate actuation or make all poses reachable.
The source states added flexibility and working volume from a gantry or mobile base.
Anthropomorphic describes the human-arm-like arrangement, not cognitive ability.
The printed course expansion is Selective Compliance Adaptive Robot Arm; the stem explicitly asks this source wording.
Under the stated serial-arm convention the last three joints form the orienting wrist.
Rigidity supports industrial accuracy; lightweight space applications can motivate flexible links or joints. Neither is universally superior.
Teach-and-playback first records manually guided positions, then replays them.
The slide lists teaching time and lack of reaction to environmental changes as limitations.
Sensor-driven decisions use sensors, whereas the intelligent mode uses AI to learn the environment; the other pairings negate those definitions.
The first fictional law prioritizes avoiding human harm over obedience and self-preservation.
With human safety stipulated, obedience under law two outranks self-preservation under law three.
A spatial pose comprises position and orientation. The other quantities are not the stated pair.
A body-fixed coordinate frame represents its pose relative to a reference frame, not observer-independent coordinates.
Kinematics studies motion without forces; velocity versus joint motion fits, actuator forces and inertia torques do not.
The source includes position, velocity and acceleration in kinematics; forces and torques belong to dynamics.
Revolute displacement is an angle; prismatic displacement is translational offset.
Joint position sensors measure the relative position of neighboring links, not arbitrary objects or costs.
Forward kinematics maps given joint coordinates to tool-frame position and orientation relative to base.
Inverse kinematics solves joint coordinates from a desired end-effector pose.
Existence and multiplicity of inverse solutions are not guaranteed. Desired poses can have no feasible, one feasible or multiple feasible configurations.
By definition of the attainable pose workspace, a pose with no feasible joint realization lies outside it under the given model.
The Jacobian maps joint velocity to Cartesian velocity locally, not directly position to mass or torque to pose.
The slide calls the velocity mapping noninvertible at singular configurations. This does not imply that every direction is lost.
The slide relation is tau equals transpose(J) times Cartesian wrench in consistent coordinates; virtual-work dimensional mapping agrees.
Direct multiplication diag(2,3) times (1,-2) yields (2,-6). No inversion or addition is needed.
Transpose J is [[1,0],[2,3]]. Multiplying by (4,5) gives (4,8+15)=(4,23), not JF=(14,15).
Dynamics adds the forces needed to cause motion, unlike force-free motion geometry.
Required torques depend on trajectory space/time, link/payload mass and joint friction. Final pose alone cannot determine the motion torque history.
Inverse dynamics maps desired motion to torques; direct dynamics maps applied torques to acceleration and resulting motion.
The coordinated timing convention starts and ends all joint motions together; displacements and torques need not be equal.
Via points are intermediate locations through which the trajectory must pass, not obstacles or only its final target.
Design geometry and joints affect workspace and structural stiffness. Color and syntax are not the stated structural outcomes.
Size, speed, load capability and joint arrangement are listed design factors.
More joints can increase dexterity but increase construction difficulty and cost; no universal accuracy or free-sensor guarantee follows.
The fourth circuit-board assembly joint rotates the held component about the vertical axis after three positioning coordinates.
The specialized placement task needs only one independent orientation angle, unlike a general three-orientation full-pose task.
Model parameters can be imperfect and disturbances remain; control compensates them rather than merely writing dynamics equations.
Joint position/velocity measurements feed the control algorithm, which computes actuator torque commands in a feedback loop.
The slide describes approximate linear control as common and nonlinear dynamics consideration as improving performance, not eliminating all uncertainty.
The source contrasts free-space position control with contact force control, while explaining complementary hybrid use.
Hybrid control assigns position and force laws to complementary directions, avoiding contradictory commands for the same constrained variable.
For wiping, normal force maintains contact while tangential motion follows the cleaning trajectory, matching the drawing arrows.
A robot language is the human-user to robot interface; it is not a mechanical replacement.
The term flexible here means programmable and must not be confused with mechanically flexible links.
The source defines an offline graphics-supported environment that permits program development without the physical robot.
The three stated benefits are avoiding production interruption, connecting CAD to manufacturing, and sometimes reducing programming time; universal physical safety is not guaranteed.
The slide explicitly lists desired motions, desired contact forces and complex manipulation strategies as language-expressible commands.
